The Tropical screech owl Megascops choliba is a widespread neotropical strigid that inhabits a diverse array of forested and semi-open habitats from Costa Rica south to northern Argentina. Field studies have documented its basic life-history parameters, providing valuable data for comparative analyses of avian reproductive strategies. Eggs are incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], and the total incubation period yields an age at hatching of 26 days [ab = 26 days], a duration that is consistent with values reported for other small-bodied otus-like owls. Newly hatched nestlings, which are altricial and initially covered in sparse down, exhibit a wet weight at birth of 12 grams [Wwb = 12 grams], a relatively modest mass that reflects the substantial yolk investment required for rapid early growth. The initial weight of the freshly laid egg has been measured at 16.6 grams [Ww0 = 16.6 grams], though a separate study by Guilherme and Souza (2017) reported a slightly lower mean value of 15 grams [Ww0 = 15 grams] with a standard deviation of 1 gram, indicating some intraspecific variation potentially linked to maternal age or local food availability.

Under the ambient thermal conditions typical of active roosting and nocturnal foraging periods in this species, which average 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a predictable sequence of post-hatching developmental milestones unfolds. Fledging, marked by the achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest cavity, occurs at 30 days after hatching [tx = 30 days after hatching], an interval that is relatively short compared to larger strigids and likely reflects selective pressures for rapid independence in a variable tropical environment at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Sexual maturation, characterized by the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the production of viable gametes, follows considerably later, with puberty estimated at 90 days after hatching [tp = 90 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This delay between fledging and reproductive activation is a common pattern among altricial birds, allowing the immature individual to complete skeletal growth and develop proficient hunting skills before committing resources to reproduction.

Under the thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], which corresponds to the elevated body temperature maintained during active hunting periods, the time interval since birth at which a female produces her first brood is approximately 365 days [tR = approximately 365 days], indicating that first reproduction typically occurs in the second calendar year of life following a prolonged period of post-fledging maturation and territory establishment. Adult females lay between 2 and 3 eggs per single clutch [N_R_i = between 2 and 3 eggs per single clutch], and typically only a single clutch is produced each year [F_R_i = single clutch is produced each year], a conservative frequency that contrasts with the multiple nesting attempts observed in some temperate strigids. The reproductive output of the Tropical screech owl is typical of a small, multiple-brooded tropical owl, reflecting a strategy that balances high offspring quality with a modest annual investment.

Adult body size in this species exhibits a moderate degree of sexual dimorphism, with females attaining a larger ultimate wet weight than males, a pattern that is widespread among raptorial birds and is hypothesized to facilitate the egg-carrying and brooding duties of the female. The maximum recorded body mass for adult females is 148 grams [Wwi = 148 grams], whereas adult males, which are the primary providers of food to the incubating female and the early nestlings, reach a typical asymptotic mass of 138 grams [Wwi = 138 grams]. This 10-gram difference in body mass is consistent with the reversed sexual size dimorphism observed across the genus Megascops and related otus-owl clades, and it may also confer advantages during aggressive intersexual interactions over nest sites in the densely wooded habitats that this species prefers.

Longevity records for the Tropical screech owl are limited, but available data from banding studies and captive populations, when extrapolated under the species typical active metabolic temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 20.7 years [am = approximately 20.7 years], a figure that aligns closely with the long lifespans documented in congeneric species such as the Eastern screech owl Megascops asio. Such extended longevity is characteristic of small, cavity-nesting strigids that face relatively low adult mortality rates through the use of protected roost sites and a generalized, ambush-based hunting strategy. This long adult lifespan, combined with the modest annual reproductive output of a single clutch containing 2 to 3 eggs, positions the species firmly within the slow end of the avian life-history continuum, where delayed reproduction and high adult survival are favored under the relatively stable environmental conditions of its tropical and subtropical range.
